title: Concurrency Control
summary: When many transactions run at once, data can corrupt silently. Learn the protocols databases use to keep reads and writes correct.

blocks.markdown:
A database runs many **transactions** simultaneously. Without control, they interfere — reads see partial writes, updates overwrite each other.

- **Concurrency control** is the set of mechanisms that keeps concurrent transactions correct.
- Correctness means the schedule is **serializable**: equivalent to some serial order. See [serializability-recoverability](serializability-recoverability).
- Three main families: **lock-based**, **timestamp ordering**, and **optimistic** (validation-based).
- Most real databases layer all three. See [transactions-acid](transactions-acid).

blocks.subTitle: Lost update
blocks.markdown:
A **lost update** happens when two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value, and the second write silently erases the first.

Example: both transactions read balance = 100. T1 writes 110, T2 writes 90 — T1's +10 is gone.

- The database ends up in a state neither transaction intended.
- Any correct protocol must prevent this.

blocks.subTitle: Dirty read & unrepeatable read
blocks.markdown:
Two more classic anomalies:

- **Dirty read** — T2 reads a value written by T1 **before T1 commits**. If T1 rolls back, T2 acted on data that never existed.
- **Unrepeatable read** — T2 reads a row, T1 updates and commits it, T2 reads the same row again and gets a different value in the same transaction.

See [isolation-levels](isolation-levels) for which anomalies each isolation level allows.

blocks.subTitle: Shared and exclusive locks
blocks.markdown:
**Lock-based** control lets transactions declare intent before accessing data.

- **Shared (S) lock** — granted for reads. Many transactions can hold an S lock on the same item simultaneously.
- **Exclusive (X) lock** — granted for writes. Only one transaction holds it; no other S or X lock allowed.

Compatibility rule: S+S is fine; S+X or X+X blocks. A transaction must wait if the lock conflicts.

blocks.subTitle: Two-phase locking (2PL)
blocks.markdown:
**Two-phase locking (2PL)** is the classic protocol that guarantees serializability using locks.

- **Growing phase** — a transaction acquires locks and never releases any.
- **Shrinking phase** — once it releases the first lock it can only release; no new locks allowed.

The two-phase discipline ensures the schedule is equivalent to running transactions one at a time. The moment a lock is released marks the **lock point** — the transaction's position in the serial order.

blocks.subTitle: 2PL variants
blocks.markdown:
Basic 2PL guarantees serializability but not recoverability. Three stricter variants fix that:

- **Strict 2PL** — release exclusive (write) locks only **at commit/abort**. Prevents dirty reads; used by most DBs.
- **Rigorous 2PL** — release **all** locks (S and X) only at commit/abort. Simpler to implement; serial order = commit order.
- **Conservative (static) 2PL** — acquire **all** needed locks before the transaction starts. No deadlocks but requires knowing the read/write set upfront.

**Timestamp ordering (TO)** avoids locks entirely. Each transaction T gets a timestamp TS(T) at start. Each data item X tracks:

- `read_TS(X)` — largest TS that read X.
- `write_TS(X)` — largest TS that wrote X.

Rule: an operation is allowed only if it respects the timestamp order. Violating transactions are **rolled back and restarted** with a newer timestamp — no waiting, no deadlocks, but more restarts under high contention.

**Optimistic concurrency control (OCC)** assumes conflicts are rare and checks only at the end.

Three phases per transaction:
1. **Read** — execute against a private copy; write to a local buffer, not the DB.
2. **Validate** — check whether any concurrent committed transaction conflicts.
3. **Write** — if validation passes, apply the local writes; otherwise abort and retry.

Low overhead when conflicts are rare (read-heavy workloads); wastes work when contention is high.

Locking row-by-row is expensive for bulk operations; locking the whole table blocks small reads. **Multiple granularity locking** lets transactions lock at any level of a hierarchy: database → table → page → row.

**Intention locks** signal intent before taking a fine-grained lock:
- **IS** (intention shared) — will read some descendant.
- **IX** (intention exclusive) — will write some descendant.
- **SIX** (shared + IX) — reads the whole node, writes some descendants.

Before locking a node, the transaction sets the corresponding intention lock on all ancestors. Coarse-grained operations stay fast; fine-grained ones still work concurrently.

**Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC)** keeps multiple versions of each data item. When a transaction writes, it creates a **new version** rather than overwriting.

- **Readers** see the snapshot valid at their transaction's start timestamp — they never block writers.
- **Writers** never block readers.
- Old versions are cleaned up by a background **vacuum** process when no transaction needs them anymore.

Used by PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle. The main cost is storage for old versions and vacuum overhead.

Pick the approach by contention and workload.

| Protocol | On conflict | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| 2PL | Waits (deadlock risk) | Mixed read/write |
| Timestamp | Restarts (no deadlock) | High-contention reads |
| OCC | Retries at end | Read-heavy, rare conflicts |
| MVCC | Readers never block | Snapshot-heavy workloads |

Most production databases combine strict 2PL for writes with MVCC for reads.

Common mistakes:

- **"2PL prevents all anomalies."** Basic 2PL guarantees serializability but not recoverability — cascading aborts can still happen. Use **strict 2PL**.
- **"MVCC means no locks ever."** Writes in MVCC still need exclusive locks or compare-and-swap; only reads avoid blocking.
- **"Optimistic is always faster."** OCC wastes work on aborted transactions. Under high write contention, pessimistic locking wins.
- **"Deadlocks are rare; ignore them."** Any lock-based system needs deadlock detection or a timeout policy. See [deadlock-handling](deadlock-handling).

blocks.subTitle: What is two-phase locking?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is two-phase locking and why does it guarantee serializability?**

2PL splits a transaction into a **growing phase** (acquire locks only) and a **shrinking phase** (release locks only). Because no lock is released until after all acquisitions, the order of lock points defines a valid serial execution order — proven by the fact that no cycles can form in the precedence graph.

blocks.subTitle: Shared vs exclusive lock
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock?**

A **shared (S) lock** allows concurrent reads — many transactions can hold it at once. An **exclusive (X) lock** is for writes — only one holder, and it blocks all other S and X requests. The rule: S+S compatible, everything else conflicts.

blocks.subTitle: How MVCC avoids blocking readers
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does MVCC let readers avoid blocking writers?**

Each write creates a **new version** of the row. Readers see the snapshot that was current at their transaction start — they read an older version while the writer works on the new one. No shared lock needed; reader and writer touch different versions of the same data.

blocks.subTitle: Optimistic vs pessimistic
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: When would you choose optimistic over pessimistic concurrency control?**

**Pessimistic** (locks) pays the lock overhead upfront but never wastes committed work. Choose it when conflicts are frequent (high-write workloads). **Optimistic** pays nothing upfront but aborts and retries on conflict — choose it when conflicts are rare (read-heavy, low-contention). Most databases default to pessimistic writes with optimistic reads via MVCC.
